newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NEW SYSTEM COULD REVAMP CHAOTIC S.AFRICAN CUSTOMS.
newsitem.headline: NEW SYSTEM COULD REVAMP CHAOTIC S.AFRICAN CUSTOMS.

text.p: A new system aimed at overhauling South Africa's shambolic customs and excise controls has been designed and could be phased in over the next three years, according to its backers.
South Africa loses billions of rand each year in revenue through corruption and fraud at its ports, a problem which has been compounded by understaffing and poor technology.

The Technological Information Management System, developed by private firm IPES and now being assessed by officials, would initially link databases at the Department of Trade and Industry, port authority Portnet and Customs and Excise.
It would introduce information such as transaction statistics, a bar code system providing container information as well as a tracking system using terrestrial radio and satellite tracking.
A scanning mechanism and a software package aimed at providing real time data on the movement of imports and exports is also planned.

An initial phase, which would focus on customs law enforcement at four transport hubs -- Durban, Cape Town, City Deep in Johannesburg and Beit Bridge on the border of South Africa and Zimbabwe -- would take four months to implement.
Leon Vermaak, the designer of the system, said the development of the system stemmed from the need to eradicate South Africa's reputation of being a smuggler's dream.
"South Africa has become a smuggler's den and could easily gain the reputation of being the smuggler's capital of the world because of the near collapse of customs control," Vermaak said.
It also took cognisance of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's recent statement that no industrial policy could have integrity until the country had efficient customs control.

Vermaak said lax customs controls cost South Africa some five billion rand a year in lost Value Added Tax receipts as well as providing a fillip for a burgeoning grey import market -- estimated to be a 12 billion rand a year industry.
Ben van Rensburg, senior economist at the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob), put the total loss of tax revenue at something between 12 and 20 billion rand a year.
"A linked database system will start to solve this specific problem because it will give you those linkages between importation, customs and excise, VAT, and income tax," Van Rensburg said.
An advantage of the system would be that it would improve the reliability of South African trade data -- lambasted by economists recently as unreliable.
"Our import and export numbers have become almost the laughing stock of the financial world. We know that those numbers are not to be trusted," van Rensburg said.
"We think that putting a proper, trustworthy database in place and which we know good data is coming in and out is a starting point of solving the problem," he added.
Vermaak said the system has already been presented to most of the stakeholders and the private sector who had approved the concept in principle.
High level talks are currently underway to discuss the financing of the project which is expected to result in a decision being made on whether government or the private sector will fund the scheme.
